title: Nanjing massacre
summary: Japanese forces began a massacre of Chinese civilians and unarmed soldiers in Nanjing on 13 December 1937 that, per People's Daily, lasted over six weeks. Death tolls depend on who counts and on scope. People's Daily gives more than 300,000; historian Kasahara Tokushi estimated 100,000–200,000 killed in Nanjing and its six counties between 4 December 1937 and 28 March 1938.

uncertainty.note: Start is 13 December 1937 (People's Daily). Kasahara's wider definition runs 4 December 1937–28 March 1938.

as_recorded.value: On Dec. 13, 1937, the invading Japanese army launched a massacre in Nanjing lasting over six weeks
from December 4, 1937, until March 28, 1938 (Kasahara Tokushi’s definition)

when.display: From 13 December 1937 (over six weeks; wider scholarly scope to 28 March 1938)

where.historical_name: Nanjing (Nanking in a 1938 New York Times headline), China

importance.justification: A heavily documented mass killing of civilians in East Asia during the Second World War; its toll and memory remain disputed (Asia-Pacific Journal).

audience_note: This record concerns mass killing of civilians and prisoners. Figures are contested and depend on place and period counted; People’s Daily is a Chinese state newspaper.

sources.title: When numbers speak: Key facts on the Nanjing Massacre
sources.author: Wu Chaolan, Zhang Kaiwei

sources.title: The Nanjing Massacre. Changing Contours of History and Memory in Japan, China, and the U.S.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the death toll: only two attributed figures were opened (PRC state press 300,000+, Kasahara 100,000–200,000); the Tokyo and Nanjing tribunal figures were not on an opened page so are omitted. Durdin's 33,000 refers to the battle only. No polity named for the city because no opened page states it.
